name: Babchi (Psoralea corylifolia)
short: Case reports: fatal acute liver failure after a multi-herb tablet containing babchi seed; acute hepatitis; a severe phototoxic reaction. One hospital: 40 of 547 drug liver injuries attributed to it.
text: Liver injury is documented mainly in case reports and case series. A case report described a 53-year-old woman with vitiligo who developed acute cholestatic hepatitis after about 7 months of a five-herb tablet in which the seed of this plant is a main ingredient, and who died 5 days after admission from acute liver failure and multiple organ dysfunction; other case reports describe acute cholestatic hepatitis in a postmenopausal woman who took the seeds in amounts over 10 times the usual dose, and three cases of acute hepatitis after the seeds or a related proprietary medicine. In a review of 547 patients with drug-induced liver injury at one Beijing hospital from 2005 to 2017, 40 cases (7.3%) were attributed to this herb (as Bu Gu Zhi, taken mainly for osteoporosis), mostly women; 11 were classed as severe, 37 recovered within 6 months, and none died or needed a transplant. For the skin, case reports describe a severe phototoxic reaction to the seeds in a child with vitiligo (the record has no abstract, so the route is not given) and phytophotodermatitis after the seeds were applied to the skin for vitiligo, and a systematic review of plants used for vitiligo lists reports of blistering, erythema, acute hepatitis and mutagenesis with this plant. A further case report described severe liver injury, taking about nine months to return to normal, in a 3-year-old boy after a concentrated psoralen-containing tincture was applied around his mouth for about one month, with suspected accidental swallowing; the background of that report states that modern studies have shown that the plant's active constituents may possess hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity (kidney toxicity). No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
